# `allodb` for Biomass

```{r, include=F, warning=F, message=F, eval = F}

validation_trees %>% 
  sf::st_transform(crs = sf::st_crs(4326)) %>% 
  dplyr::mutate(
    tree_lon = sf::st_coordinates(.)[,1]
    , tree_lat = sf::st_coordinates(.)[,2]

      # https://gdam-api-v2-782971006568.us-west1.run.app/docs#/Index/index

  ) %>% 
  dplyr::slice_sample(n=44) %>% 
  dplyr::slice_head(n=7) %>% 
  sf::st_drop_geometry() %>% 
  dplyr::select(fastfuels_api)
```

now that we have a species classification framework, We will test out a method for attaching biomass in kg to the spatial tree list from `cloud2trees`:

1. Estimate single tree biomass (kg) using allometric equations based on predictors such as tree diameter, height, and species
    + This methodology is well represented in the literature with allometries developed for nearly all tree species ([Chojnacky et al. 2014](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?cluster=13769102016905655949&hl=en&as_sdt=0,5); [Ter-Mikaelian & Korzukhin 1997](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?cluster=6148302766104288498&hl=en&as_sdt=0,5))
    + [Gonzalez‐Akre et al. (2022)](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?cluster=14167690887599848846&oi=gsb&hl=en&as_sdt=0,5) developed an R package to perform this exact task: [`allodb`](https://github.com/ropensci/allodb).

```{r, include=F, eval=F}
ref_trees_list <- list()
ref_trees_list[["usfs_manitouef_n1"]] <- usfs_manitouef_n1_trees %>% dplyr::slice_sample(n = 222)
ref_trees_list[["usfs_manitouef_bigplot"]] <- usfs_manitouef_bigplot_trees %>% 
  dplyr::slice_sample(n = 333) %>% 
  dplyr::mutate(
    species_symbol = ifelse(species_symbol=="POTR","POTR5",species_symbol)
    , species_symbol = ifelse(species_symbol=="PIFL","PIFL2",species_symbol)
  )
ref_trees_list[["usfs_manitouef_bigplot"]] %>% sf::st_drop_geometry() %>% dplyr::count(species_symbol)
ref_trees_list[["usfs_manitouef_n1"]] %>% dplyr::glimpse()
```

```{r}
library(allodb)
```

we'll start by using the FIA species code lookup table to get genus and species for all of our data sets based on the `species_symbol` (e.g. "PIPO", "POTR5", "QURU")

```{r}
# ref_trees_list
ref_trees_list <- 
  ref_trees_list %>% 
  purrr::map(
    \(df)
    df %>% 
      # get rid of columns we'll create
      dplyr::select( -dplyr::any_of(c(
        "hey_xxxxxxxxxx"
        , "genus"
        , "species"
        , "common_name"
      ))) %>% 
      dplyr::left_join(
        fia_species_lookup %>% 
          dplyr::select(
            species_symbol
            , genus
            , species
            , common_name
          )
        , by = "species_symbol"
        , relationship = "many-to-one"
      )
  )
# pred_trees_list
pred_trees_list <- 
  pred_trees_list %>% 
  purrr::map(
    \(df)
    df %>% 
      # get rid of columns we'll create
      dplyr::select( -dplyr::any_of(c(
        "hey_xxxxxxxxxx"
        , "genus"
        , "species"
        , "common_name"
      ))) %>% 
      dplyr::left_join(
        fia_species_lookup %>% 
          dplyr::select(
            species_symbol
            , genus
            , species
            , common_name
          )
        , by = "species_symbol"
        , relationship = "many-to-one"
      )
  )
```


let's take the `allodb::get_biomass()` function for a spin, demonstrating with the first study site: `r names(ref_trees_list)[1]`. 

required inputs for this function are: 

* `dbh`	- a numeric vector containing tree diameter at breast height (dbh) measurements, in cm.
* `genus` - a character vector (same length as dbh), containing the genus (e.g. "Quercus") of each tree.
* `coords` - a numeric vector of length 2 with longitude and latitude (if all trees were measured in the same location) or a matrix with 2 numerical columns giving the coordinates of each tree.
* `species` - a character vector (same length as dbh), containing the species (e.g. "rubra") of each tree. Default is NULL, when no species identification is available.

The function returns "A numeric vector of the same length as dbh, containing AGB value (in kg) for every stem."

this documentation is particularly interesting for noting that only `genus` is required and `species` is optional. based on the accuracy evaluation of the proposed classification method we just reviewed, we found that genus-level accuracy was generally higher, sometimes significantly higher, than species-level classification

```{r}
# ?allodb::get_biomass
ref_trees_list <- 
  ref_trees_list %>% 
  purrr::map(function(df){
    df$allodb_agb_kg <- allodb::get_biomass(
        dbh = df$dbh_cm
        , genus = df$genus
        , species = df$species
        , coords = 
          df %>%
            sf::st_transform(crs = sf::st_crs(4326)) %>%
            sf::st_coordinates() %>% 
            dplyr::as_tibble()
      )
    return(df)
  })

```

what did we get back?

```{r, results='asis'}
# fia_species_lookup %>% dplyr::filter(stringr::str_starts(species_symbol,"PIFL"))
ref_trees_list[[1]] %>%

  knitr::kable(format = "markdown")
```

let's plot estimated total aboveground biomass (kg) versus DBH

```{r}
ref_trees_list[[1]] %>% 
  ggplot2::ggplot(
    mapping = ggplot2::aes(x = dbh_cm, y = allodb_agb_kg, color = genus)
  ) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(size=3, alpha=0.8) +
  ggplot2::facet_wrap(facets = dplyr::vars(genus)) +
  ggplot2::scale_color_viridis_d(option="turbo") +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  ggplot2::scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "DBH (cm)", y = "AGB (kg)") +
  ggplot2::theme_light() +
  ggplot2::theme(legend.position = "top")

```

```{r, include = F, eval = F}
ref_trees_list[[1]] %>% 
  ggplot2::ggplot(
    mapping = ggplot2::aes(x = dbh_cm, y = allodb_agb_kg, color = genus)
  ) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(size=3, alpha=0.8) +
  ggplot2::facet_wrap(facets = dplyr::vars(species_symbol), ncol = 3) +
  ggplot2::scale_color_viridis_d(option="turbo") +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  ggplot2::scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "DBH (cm)", y = "AGB (kg)") +
  ggplot2::theme_light() +
  ggplot2::theme(legend.position = "top")

```
